what_it_does: CGRAs — coarse-grained reconfigurable arrays — are chips made of a grid of small, reusable computing blocks that can be rewired in software, making them very energy-efficient for workloads that repeat the same math in nested loops (like image processing or neural networks). The problem is that programming a CGRA today is painful: developers must manually figure out how to map their loops onto the grid and how to pipeline multiple loops so they overlap in time. The Adora compiler automates this entire flow — it takes a high-level algorithm, works out the best way to assign loops to the CGRA's blocks, and schedules overlapping tasks so the chip stays busy. The key claim is that this is done end-to-end with minimal hand-tuning, opening CGRAs to a wider range of software developers. Because this summary is based only on the abstract, the exact performance gains and hardware targets are not confirmed here.
